subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: The unit builds three big skills. Second, you learn to build programs that have more than one character, where some sprites have code and some are static objects (sprites that just sit there with no code, like a tree in the background). Third, you learn to make changes to your code to get the result they want — making a character talk for longer, changing the scene, or fixing a story whose steps are out of order.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Use logical thinking to put the parts of a story in an order that makes sense.
Plan a simple story on a storyboard — a beginning, a middle and an end.
Choose sprites (characters) and a backdrop (the setting) in Scratch.
Build a program using when green flag clicked, say ( ) for ( ) seconds and switch backdrop to ( ).
Make two characters take turns to talk by using wait ( ) seconds.
Include a static object — a sprite that has no code — in a program.
Make changes to code to get the right result (talk for longer, change the scene, change the timing).
Find and fix a story whose steps are out of order.

concepts.title: Logical thinking: putting a story in order
concepts.explanation:
Every good story has an order. It has a beginning, a middle and an end, and the parts must go in an order that makes sense. Working out that order is called logical thinking. If the parts are jumbled, the story does not make sense.

Listen to this story. 'They became good friends. A new girl came to Ehel Academy. Sami said hello to her.' That is all muddled up!
concepts.example: It does not make sense. Let us use our clever thinking — logical thinking — to put it in the right order.
concepts.checkYourself: you cannot be friends before you have met. Can you arrange the parts so the story makes sense?

concepts.title: Plan your story: the storyboard
concepts.explanation:
Before we build a story on the computer, we plan it. A storyboard is a plan drawn in boxes, one box for each scene. It shows what we want to make before we make it.

The people who make cartoons and films do not just start drawing. First you draw a storyboard — little boxes that show each part of the story. Today we are going to plan our story the same way.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: plan your story: the storyboard. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Does the storyboard have three scenes with a clear beginning, middle and end? The drawings do not need to be neat — quick stick figures are perfect. For each scene, can you name a character and a setting?

concepts.title: Meet Scratch: sprites, backdrops and the say block
concepts.explanation:
Now we open Scratch and meet the tools. A sprite is a character. A backdrop is the picture behind the sprites. The when green flag clicked block starts our story. The say ( ) for ( ) seconds block makes a sprite show a speech bubble. And a static object is simply a sprite that has no code — it just stands there.

concepts.example: Do it yourself: meet Scratch: sprites, backdrops and the say block. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drag and join blocks and run the program with the green flag? Can you point to the tree and say it is a static object because it has no code? Can you add a sprite and choose a backdrop?

concepts.title: Two characters talking: taking turns and fixing the order
concepts.explanation:
A conversation is two characters taking turns to talk. In Scratch, each sprite has its own stack of blocks, and clicking the green flag starts them all at the same time. So if we are not careful, both characters talk at once. To make them take turns, we add a wait ( ) seconds block so one character waits quietly while the other one speaks.

Act it out first with no computer. See how they took turns?
concepts.example: They did not talk over each other. Our sprites need to take turns too, so one of them has to wait.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you keep the when green flag clicked block at the top? Can you reorder a jumbled conversation so it makes sense? Does you use a wait block so the characters do not talk over each other?

concepts.title: Making changes and switching scenes
concepts.explanation:
We can change our code to get the result we want. If we change the number in say ( ) for (2) seconds to (4), the character talks for twice as long. If we change the wait times, the conversation goes faster or slower. And if we add a switch backdrop to ( ) block, our story moves to a new scene. Small changes make a big difference.

Let us make Maya talk for longer. Then add a second scene. First add a second backdrop (for example Room 1) using Choose a Backdrop, then add a switch backdrop to ( ) block so the story moves indoors Take yesterday's greeting.
concepts.example: Find one real example of making changes and switching scenes around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you add a second backdrop and a switch backdrop to ( ) block? Can you include a static object (a sprite with no code)? Does you change a number and then run the program to check the result?

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in two characters talking: taking turns and fixing the order, and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A conversation is two characters taking turns to talk. In Scratch, each sprite has its own stack of blocks, and clicking the green flag starts them all at the same time. So if we are not careful, both characters talk at once. To make them take turns, we add a wait ( ) seconds block so one character waits quietly while the other one speaks.

Act it out first with no computer. See how they took turns?

project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Storyteller into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a storyteller project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.

When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I planned my story on the storyboard.
I added two sprites and two backdrops.
My two friends take turns to talk (they do not talk at the same time).

My scene changes from the playground to the room.
I made one change to my code and tested it with the green flag.

selfAssessment: I can use logical thinking to put the parts of a story in an order that makes sense.
I can plan a simple story on a storyboard — a beginning, a middle and an end.
I can choose sprites (characters) and a backdrop (the setting) in Scratch.
I can build a program using when green flag clicked, say ( ) for ( ) seconds and switch backdrop to ( ).
I can make two characters take turns to talk by using wait ( ) seconds.
I can include a static object — a sprite that has no code — in a program.
I can make changes to code to get the right result (talk for longer, change the scene, change the timing).
I can find and fix a story whose steps are out of order.
